- If sentiment shows strong positive change followed by a sharp drop, model tends to overreact and overshoot — reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- When sentiment is consistently low or negative over recent days, model often underestimates downside risk — add 2–5% buffer to forecast for downward correction.
- If news volume is low but sentiment is high, model overestimates momentum — dampen forecast by 3–8% to avoid overconfidence bias.
- Model tends to lag in correcting for sentiment reversals — if sentiment turns negative after a spike, delay forecast adjustment by 1–2 days and reduce slope.
- In high-news-volume periods, model often overfits short-term volatility — apply smoothing filter to reduce 3–5% peak overshoot.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion after a spike, model often fails to recognize it — adjust forecast to align with 20–30-day moving average of history.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral, model tends to overpredict volatility — reduce forecast variance by 10–20% to reflect low sentiment-driven noise.
- If sentiment change is negative and forecast is rising, model often misreads sentiment — reduce forecast slope by 15–25% to avoid false momentum.
